blocks.text: Cross-entropy measures the gap between a true probability distribution and a predicted one, and it is the single most widely used loss function for training classification models, from a simple logistic regression to the largest language models in production today.

1. What Cross-Entropy Measures

Where entropy, covered in the previous lesson, measures the uncertainty within a single distribution, cross-entropy measures how well a predicted distribution matches a true one. A model that assigns high probability to the actual correct class produces low cross-entropy, while a model that confidently predicts the wrong class produces high cross-entropy.

Whenever cross-entropy is quoted as a single number for a model, lower always means better, a predicted distribution closer to the truth, while a higher value signals a predicted distribution drifting further from what actually happened.

Cross-entropy always requires two distributions over the exact same set of possible outcomes, comparing a prediction against a true label that lists a completely different set of categories is not a meaningful operation.
2. The Formula

Cross-entropy is defined as H(P, Q) = negative sum over all outcomes of p(x) times log2 q(x), where P is the true distribution and Q is the predicted distribution. Notice the log is applied to the predicted probability q, while the weighting still comes from the true probability p.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: When the true label is one-hot encoded, only one term in the sum survives, since every other true probability is exactly 0 and contributes nothing, simplifying the calculation to just negative log2 of the predicted probability assigned to the single correct class.

blocks.text: Some libraries use natural log instead of log base 2 in this formula, changing the numeric scale of the loss value from bits to nats, without changing which model is judged better relative to another.
3. Why It Is the Standard Classification Loss

Cross-entropy loss, sometimes called log loss, penalizes a confident wrong prediction far more heavily than a mildly wrong one, since the negative log of a probability near 0 grows enormously large. This sharp penalty pushes a model to become genuinely well calibrated, assigning high probability specifically to the correct class, rather than merely getting the top prediction right by chance.

code.content:
print(cross_entropy([1, 0, 0], [0.9, 0.05, 0.05]))   # small loss, confident and correct
print(cross_entropy([1, 0, 0], [0.1, 0.8, 0.1]))     # large loss, confident and wrong

blocks.text: This calibration pressure is a genuinely useful side effect, a well trained classifier using cross-entropy loss tends to produce probability outputs that meaningfully reflect true confidence, not just a ranking of which class is most likely.

Compare this against a simpler alternative like counting the number of correct predictions directly, which gives no useful signal at all for adjusting model parameters gradually during training, exactly why cross-entropy, not accuracy, is used as the actual training objective.
4. The Connection to Entropy

Cross-entropy can always be split into two pieces, H(P, Q) = H(P) + KL(P, Q), the entropy of the true distribution plus the KL divergence between the true and predicted distributions, covered fully in the next lesson. Since H(P) is fixed by the data and does not depend on the model, minimizing cross-entropy during training is exactly equivalent to minimizing KL divergence.

This split also explains why cross-entropy can never be smaller than plain entropy, KL divergence is always non-negative, covered in full in the next lesson, so the smallest cross-entropy achievable is exactly the entropy of the true distribution itself, reached only when the prediction matches it perfectly.

This relationship is one of the cleanest, most useful identities in the whole information theory module, connecting the uncertainty measure from the previous lesson directly to both the loss function covered here and the divergence measure covered next.
5. A Worked Multi-Class Example
A 3-class classifier predicts probabilities 0.7, 0.2, 0.1 for classes cat, dog, and bird, and the true label is cat, one-hot encoded as [1, 0, 0]. Compute the cross-entropy loss.

code.content:
true_label = [1, 0, 0]
predicted = [0.7, 0.2, 0.1]
loss = cross_entropy(true_label, predicted)
print(loss)   # about 0.5146 bits

blocks.content: {"headers":["Class","True","Predicted","Contribution"],"rows":[["Cat","1","0.7","negative log2(0.7), about 0.5146"],["Dog","0","0.2","0, since true probability is 0"],["Bird","0","0.1","0, since true probability is 0"]]}

blocks.text: Only the cat row contributes anything to the total loss, since dog and bird both have a true probability of 0, which zeroes out their entire term in the sum regardless of what the model predicted for them.

If the model instead predicted 0.9 for cat, the loss would shrink further to about 0.152, confirming directly that assigning even more probability to the correct class always reduces the cross-entropy loss.
6. Binary Cross-Entropy

For a two-class problem, cross-entropy simplifies to negative (y times log(p) plus (1 minus y) times log(1 minus p)), where y is the true label, 0 or 1, and p is the predicted probability of the positive class. This binary form is the standard loss function for logistic regression and binary classifiers.

Binary cross-entropy is really just the 2-class version of the general multi-class formula, written out in a slightly different, more compact form specifically because only one probability value, p, needs to be tracked instead of a full list.
Binary cross-entropy remains the standard choice for any single yes or no prediction task, spam detection, fraud detection, or medical diagnosis screening among the most common examples.
7. Cross-Entropy in Code Frameworks

Deep learning frameworks implement cross-entropy loss directly, usually combining it with the softmax function internally for numerical stability, rather than requiring predictions to already be normalized probabilities.

code.content:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
logits = torch.tensor([[2.0, 0.5, 0.1]])   # raw scores, not yet probabilities
target = torch.tensor([0])                 # correct class index
print(loss_fn(logits, target))

blocks.text: Passing already-softmaxed probabilities into a framework loss function that expects raw logits is a common, hard to notice bug, since it silently applies softmax a second time and distorts the gradient computation.

This internal combination of softmax and cross-entropy is exactly why PyTorch CrossEntropyLoss expects raw, unnormalized logits as input rather than already-softmaxed probabilities, a detail worth double checking whenever plugging a new model output into an existing training loop.
8. Why Confident Wrong Predictions Are Punished Heavily

The negative log function grows without bound as its input approaches 0, meaning a model that assigns near-zero probability to the actual correct class incurs an enormous loss, far larger than the loss from a merely uncertain, hedge-your-bets prediction. This asymmetric penalty is precisely what discourages overconfident, badly wrong predictions during training.

code.content:
print(-np.log2(0.5))     # 1 bit, uncertain prediction
print(-np.log2(0.01))    # about 6.6 bits, confidently wrong
print(-np.log2(0.0001))  # about 13.3 bits, extremely confidently wrong

blocks.text: This steep growth near zero is a deliberate, useful property, not an accident, it means the loss landscape gives a strong gradient signal to correct badly wrong, overconfident predictions quickly during training.

This behavior contrasts sharply with a simpler error measure like plain squared difference, which would treat a confident wrong prediction only mildly more harshly than a mildly wrong one, missing the sharp penalty cross-entropy provides.
9. Cross-Entropy in AI Practice

items: Nearly every image, text, and tabular data classifier trains against cross-entropy loss, from simple logistic regression to large transformer based classifiers.
Language models predict the next token by minimizing cross-entropy between their predicted vocabulary distribution and the actual next word in the training text.
Cross-entropy is the mathematical basis behind perplexity, covered in a later lesson, the standard way language models are evaluated.

blocks.text: Whenever a training log reports a decreasing loss value over time for a classification model, that value is almost always cross-entropy, watching it fall is a direct, moment to moment signal that the model predicted distribution is converging toward the true one.

Object detection and segmentation models also rely on cross-entropy for their classification component, even though they combine it with other loss terms for localizing where an object sits within an image.
10. Numerical Stability: The Softmax and Log-Sum-Exp Trick

Computing softmax followed by log directly can suffer from floating point overflow when raw scores are large, since exponentiating a large number can produce infinity. Frameworks avoid this by combining softmax and cross-entropy into a single, numerically stable operation using a technique called the log-sum-exp trick, which subtracts the maximum score before exponentiating.

This is exactly why deep learning frameworks provide a combined softmax-plus-cross-entropy function rather than two separate steps, letting the library apply this numerical safeguard internally rather than leaving it to every user to remember.
Subtracting the maximum value before exponentiating never changes the final softmax output mathematically, it only keeps the intermediate numbers within a safe range for floating point arithmetic.
11. Label Smoothing

Label smoothing slightly softens the true one-hot label, from exactly [1, 0, 0] to something like [0.9, 0.05, 0.05], before computing cross-entropy. This prevents a model from becoming overconfident and pushing predicted probabilities all the way to 0 and 1, which can hurt generalization and calibration on new data.

code.content:
def smooth_labels(one_hot, epsilon=0.1):
    n = len(one_hot)
    return [(1 - epsilon) * v + epsilon / n for v in one_hot]

print(smooth_labels([1, 0, 0]))   # [0.9333, 0.0333, 0.0333]

blocks.text: Label smoothing is a small, cheap regularization trick, typically an epsilon of around 0.1, and it is used widely in image classification and translation models to modestly improve generalization on held out data.
Choosing too large an epsilon can hurt performance by removing too much of the useful signal the true label originally provided, a small value like 0.1 is a common, well tested default.
12. Cross-Entropy Versus Accuracy as a Training Signal

Accuracy only checks whether the single highest predicted class matches the true label, a step function that provides no useful gradient signal for training. Cross-entropy instead gives a smooth, continuously differentiable measure that rewards a model for pushing probability mass toward the correct class even before it becomes the top prediction, which is exactly why models are trained against cross-entropy while accuracy is used afterward only to report performance.

This is a broadly important pattern in machine learning worth internalizing beyond this one example, the metric used to train a model, a smooth, differentiable loss, is often deliberately different from the metric used to report its final performance, which can be a simpler, more interpretable number like accuracy.
This is worth remembering the next time a model training loss and its reported accuracy seem to move somewhat independently of each other, they are legitimately measuring two different things.
13. A Worked Example
Compute the cross-entropy loss for two competing models predicting the same 3-class example, where the true label is class B.

code.content:
true_label = [0, 1, 0]
model_a_pred = [0.1, 0.8, 0.1]
model_b_pred = [0.3, 0.4, 0.3]
print(cross_entropy(true_label, model_a_pred))   # lower loss, more confident and correct
print(cross_entropy(true_label, model_b_pred))   # higher loss, less confident

blocks.text: Notice that both models would count as correct if only accuracy were measured, since both assign the highest probability to class B, but cross-entropy correctly reveals model A as the more confident, better calibrated of the two.
14. Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting that predicted probabilities must be strictly between 0 and 1, a predicted probability of exactly 0 for the true class produces an infinite loss due to the log of zero.
Confusing cross-entropy with plain entropy, cross-entropy always requires two distributions, a true one and a predicted one, not just one.
Applying the multi-class cross-entropy formula to a binary problem without using the simplified binary form, or vice versa, leading to shape mismatches in code.
Manually applying softmax before calling a framework loss function that already applies softmax internally, silently applying it twice and corrupting the gradient.

blocks.text: A related trap worth naming directly: comparing raw cross-entropy loss values across two datasets with a different number of classes, more classes generally means a higher baseline loss even for an equally good model, since there is simply more probability mass to distribute correctly.
15. Practice: Compute Cross-Entropy Loss
A binary classifier predicts 0.85 probability of the positive class for an example whose true label is 1, and 0.3 for an example whose true label is 0. Compute the binary cross-entropy loss for both.

Compare the two resulting loss values directly, and notice how much larger the loss becomes for the second example, where the model confidently predicted the wrong class, versus the first, where it was confident and correct.
Key Takeaway

Label smoothing and the numerical stability tricks covered in sections 10 and 11 are exactly the kind of practical engineering details that separate a textbook formula from a production-ready training pipeline.

Cross-entropy measures how well a predicted probability distribution matches the true one, computed as the negative sum of true probabilities times the log of predicted probabilities. It heavily penalizes confident wrong predictions, which is exactly what makes it such an effective classification loss function.

Cross-entropy splits exactly into entropy plus KL divergence, the subject of the next lesson, and it directly underlies perplexity, the standard evaluation metric for language models covered later in this module.

The next lesson, KL divergence, isolates the second term of the entropy plus KL divergence split covered in section 4, giving a pure measure of how one distribution differs from another, independent of how much inherent uncertainty the true distribution itself contains.
